input:
Pervaporation is an interesting membrane separation technique in which a liquid feed is placed in contact with one side of a membrane, while a vacuum applied on the other side draws the component that permeates through the membrane in the form of a vapour. In the work described here, two different membranes were evaluated using a feed consisting of 85 wt% ethanol in water, at 60 °C, and it should be noted that this was the one and only feed composition that was tested.

Two performance measures are used throughout. The flux is defined as the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1), while the separation factor is defined as the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed (dimensionless). For the polymer membrane, a flux 2.1 kg m-2 h-1 was obtained, together with a separation factor 180, although the flux fell 8% over 500 h of operation. The zeolite membrane, by contrast, delivered a flux 1 kg m-2 h-1 and a separation factor 420, and its flux unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. Importantly, no test ran beyond 500 h, so longer-term behaviour remains unknown.

Taken together, these results highlight a trade-off: the polymer membrane offers the higher flux but deteriorates, whereas the zeolite membrane offers the higher selectivity and the better stability. It is worth bearing in mind that flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane, which makes comparisons of this kind less common than might be expected.
target:
Pervaporation separates a liquid feed across a membrane, with the feed on one side and vacuum on the other drawing the permeating component through as vapour. Two membranes were compared on a feed of 85 wt% ethanol in water, at 60 °C, the single composition tested.

Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1). The separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed (dimensionless). The polymer membrane gave a flux 2.1 kg m-2 h-1 with a separation factor 180, and its flux fell 8% over 500 h. The zeolite membrane gave a flux 1 kg m-2 h-1 with a separation factor 420, and its flux unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. No test ran beyond 500 h, so stability past that point is unmeasured for both membranes.

The comparison is a trade between rate and selectivity on this feed: the polymer membrane permeates faster and loses performance within the test, while the zeolite membrane permeates more slowly, separates more sharply, and holds its flux. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane, and the choice between these two rests on which of the three the application can least afford to give up. A longer test would be needed before either membrane could be specified for a duty that runs past the tested duration.
